processing: Made as other Wuyi rock teas are: shaken to partial oxidation, fired, rolled and roasted over charcoal, with the roast level left to the maker.
harvest_season: As usual for Wuyi rock teas, a spring picking, with roasting in the months that follow.
appearance_dry: Typically long, dark, twisted strips, larger than most Wuyi cultivars, with a roasted sheen.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear orange to deep amber, depending on the roast.
appearance_wet: Typically large, soft leaves with reddened edges, as is usual for Wuyi Shui Xian.
taste_profile: One seller describes a floral aroma and a sweet aftertaste. Wuyi Shui Xian in general is known for a soft, woody body with roast and mineral notes.

brewing.notes: Fully boiling water and short early steeps, as with other rock teas. Shui Xian is forgiving, and later steeps can run long.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually from the current or previous spring after roasting, as with other Wuyi rock teas. Old-bush lots are sold separately as Lao Cong Shui Xian and cost more. Both 'zhengyan' and 'lao cong' are seller's claims with no widely quoted test behind them, so ask for the location and the age of the bushes.
description:
This is Shui Xian, one of the two workhorse cultivars of the Wuyi Mountains, grown in the central 'true rock' area instead of the ground around it. The cultivar is common and the address is the point of the name.

It is made in the way usual for rock teas: shaken, partly oxidised, fired, rolled and roasted over charcoal. A heavier roast pushes it toward wood and caramel, while a lighter one leaves more of the flowers.

As with other Wuyi Shui Xian, expect a rounder, softer body than the spicier Rou Gui, with mineral notes showing under the roast. Use boiling water and keep the first steeps short. People often underestimate how many steeps it gives.

When buying, separate three claims: Shui Xian (the cultivar), zhengyan (the place) and lao cong (old bushes). A seller who can tell you which valley and how old the bushes are has given you more than one who only prints the words on a tin.
history: Little is documented about Zhengyan Shui Xian as a named tea. The name combines the Shui Xian cultivar with the zhengyan ranking used for central Wuyi tea, and it appears mainly in seller listings rather than in any older record.
